text: Imagine your sales are growing, but your profit is quietly shrinking. Often, it only shows up months later, in the monthly report.
Here is how I would find out why, on a fictional company.
Sales grew two percent, yet EBITDA fell by seventeen point six million. Where did the margin go?
First, I bring sales, cost, energy, logistics and currency data into one model.
Then I check the numbers three ways, before trusting any chart.
Next, a driver-based bridge, built customer by customer, in constant currency.
Fifteen million is the market: fibre, energy, and a weaker krona.
But price we can control. Fixed contracts lost nine million, while indexed ones gained.
Then I rank every customer by profit, after the real cost of serving them.
Twenty-nine accounts lose money. Small accounts cost seven times more to serve, per tonne.
For energy, each plant is compared, week by week, with its own seasonal baseline.
A weekly rule catches the drift in six weeks. The monthly report showed only four percent.
An AI agent drafts the monthly commentary, from verified facts only.
Every number is checked against the data, and a controller signs off.
Five initiatives, worth about eight million euros a year, each with a KPI and an owner.
